content:
Reablement is short-term support at home that helps you relearn everyday tasks, such as washing, dressing, making a drink and moving around, after a hospital stay or illness. With arthritis, a stay in hospital can leave you stiffer and weaker than before, so reablement can make a real difference to getting back to your usual routine.

This guide explains what reablement is, how to get it, what it costs, and how to make the most of it alongside your arthritis care.

What reablement is

Reablement is part of what is called intermediate care. A team, which may include support workers, occupational therapists and physiotherapists, visits you at home for a limited time, often up to six weeks. Unlike ongoing home care, the aim is to help you do things for yourself again, not to do them for you. NICE guidance on intermediate care describes it as goal-focused and time-limited.

Why it matters with arthritis

Even a few days in bed can weaken muscles and stiffen joints. Arthritis pain, new medicines and tiredness can make it harder to get going again. Reablement gives you support and practice at the time when it can help most.

How to get reablement

  • Ask the ward team, discharge coordinator or social worker before you leave hospital.
  • If you are already at home and struggling, contact your council's adult social care team or your GP.
  • Tell them about your arthritis, including which joints are affected and what was hard before you went into hospital.

What it costs

In England, reablement and intermediate care are usually free for up to six weeks. Arrangements differ in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so ask your local council or Health and Social Care Trust what applies. If you need care after reablement ends, you may be assessed for ongoing support, which may be means-tested.

Making the most of reablement

  • Agree clear goals with the team, such as making your own lunch or getting to the shop.
  • Practise between visits, not only when the team is there.
  • Keep a simple note of what went well and what was hard to share at the next visit.
  • Ask about equipment, such as a perching stool, raised toilet seat or grab rails.
  • If pain stops you practising, tell the team so they can adjust the plan or contact your GP.

For family and carers

It can be tempting to do everything for someone after hospital, but practice is part of recovery. Help with the risky parts and leave the parts the person can manage. If moving and handling is unsafe, ask the team for advice rather than lifting.

When reablement ends

Before the last visit, the team should review how you are managing. If you still need help, ask about a care needs assessment, ongoing therapy or community services. Carers can ask for a carer's assessment.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall where you may be badly hurt.
  • Get urgent advice the same day for sudden confusion, a high temperature, a hot, swollen joint with fever, or redness or discharge from a surgical wound.
  • Contact your GP or the reablement team if you are getting weaker rather than stronger, or if pain is stopping you from moving.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is reablement the same as home care?

No. Reablement is short-term and aims to help you do things yourself. Home care is ongoing support with tasks.

Can I have reablement if I was not in hospital?

Sometimes. Councils may offer it after an illness or fall at home. Ask your council or GP.

What if I need more time?

Tell the team. They can review your goals and talk about next steps.
